summary: Parrsboro lighthouse, at the end of a breakwater in Parrsboro Harbour, has stood on a concrete tower since 1980; its 1852 wooden tower was lost after a 1945 hurricane.

structures.type: octagonal wooden tower with an attached dwelling
structures.note: Lighthouse Friends says it was lost after the 1945 hurricane. The NSLPS list dates its skeletal replacement from 1941 to 1960.
Interim structure after the first tower was taken down (NSLPS gives 1941 to 1960; Lighthouse Friends does not date it).

structures.type: square concrete tower on a one-storey building
structures.note: Height from the Coast Guard's List of Lights. Lantern room removed for refurbishment in December 2018 and returned in June 2019.

access.note: Grounds open, tower closed (Lighthouse Friends). Reached by car. The breakwater can be walked from the end of Lighthouse Road, where parking is not permitted.

events.note: Octagonal wooden tower with an attached dwelling.
Temporary light shown from the new tower; the lantern room went on the following spring.
Gale of 4 October destroyed one building at the station and damaged the breastwork.
715-foot breakwater built on a $2,000 appropriation to shield the light.
Storm of 23 and 24 November washed away roughly 100 feet of the new breakwater.
Fog bell replaced the hand horn (Department report for the year ending 30 November 1905). NSLPS lists the fog bell for 1905.
Fourth-order dioptric apparatus replaced the catoptric apparatus (Department report, fiscal 1909-10). Lighthouse Friends gives 1909; NSLPS gives 1922.

Oil engines and a diaphone foghorn (Lighthouse Friends gives 1919; NSLPS gives 1917 for the diaphone). The Department's report for fiscal 1919-20 records a new wooden building and a small diaphone plant at Parrsboro.
Hurricane made the original tower lean; the keeper, Russell Spencer, stayed to put out the kerosene light.
Original tower taken down after the storm; a mast light followed (Lighthouse Friends). NSLPS dates the skeletal tower 1941 to 1960.
Station de-staffed in 1987 (Lighthouse Friends); NSLPS says automated by 1987.
Parrsboro Lighthouse Society formed to preserve the lighthouse.
Coast Guard removed the lantern room in late December 2018 for refurbishment.
New roof in spring 2019; restored lantern room returned by Coast Guard helicopter in June 2019.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Lighthouse Friends gives 1909 for the fourth-order lens. The Department's report for fiscal 1909-10 records the substitution at Parrsboro (checked on the page image), which supports 1909 and not the 1922 date in the NSLPS list. The story states both.

The Department's report for fiscal 1919-20 records a new building and a small diaphone plant at Parrsboro. That agrees with Lighthouse Friends' 1919 and not with the NSLPS date of 1917 for the diaphone.

notes_for_editor: Checked 2026-10-28 against the sources. Disagreements stated in the story: (a) site of the first light: Lighthouse Friends says a sand spit on the western side of the entrance; NSLPS says Partridge Island. (b) loss of the first tower: Lighthouse Friends and the Nova Scotia Vacation guide give a 1945 hurricane; NSLPS lists a skeletal tower from 1941 to 1960. A commercial app page (MarineRadar, not cited) repeats the 1945 date. The Spencer anecdote is known only from Lighthouse Friends and the guide, which repeats it. (c) Howard's end date: 1857 (LF) or 1855 (NSLPS). (d) Diaphone: 1917 (NSLPS), 1919 (LF, oil engines and diaphone), and a 1919-20 Department record of a new building and a small diaphone plant at Parrsboro (scan 95); the story gives all three. (e) Lens: LF 1909, supported by the Department's fiscal 1909-10 entry (scan 93, checked on the image); NSLPS 1922, not supported. Keeper names after 1911 (W. J. Simpson, J. McNamara) are from Lighthouse Friends only. The Pettis row in the 1911 table was checked on the page image (scan 244, printed p.237), and the 1905 table (scan 176, printed p.163) gives the same name and date. The 1857 inspector's report (William Condon) is known only from Lighthouse Friends' transcription; the corpus does not cover 1852 to 1900 reports for Canada. Ronald A. Wood (1963 to 1987) may be living: named only with dates from published sources, no personal detail. Lighthouse Friends and NSLPS text is copyrighted: the story uses facts and short phrases only. The Nova Scotia Vacation guide is a tourism page and is cited only for the 1945 anecdote, the county and the 2018-19 work, which Lighthouse Friends also gives.
